metadata.title: Ageing and Skills: A Review and Analysis of Skill Gain and Skill Loss Over the Lifespan and Over Time

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper synthesizes evidence and discusses how repeated cross-sectional observations from IALS (1994–1998), ALL (2003–2007), and future PIAAC waves can be used to study age-skill profiles and cohort/ageing effects. It does not provide a student-level analytic dataset construction or an explicit complex-survey weighting/replicate-weighting strategy in the text excerpt, so the specific use of ILSA/PIAAC sampling weights cannot be verified here. For analysts using the underlying ILSA/PIAAC microdata, standard practice is to apply the provided sampling weights and replicate weights (if available) to account for stratification and clustering in the survey design. Because this paper is primarily a review and conceptual/overview analysis, it does not document the exact weight variables or replicate procedures used in any re-analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper is a review and conceptual overview that summarizes evidence and describes how trend data from IALS/ALL/PIAAC could be used to estimate skill gain and loss; it does not report an ML analysis with a PV-based cognitive achievement dependent variable. As a result, plausible-value handling and missing-data handling for an empirical predictive model are not applicable in the way they would be for an achievement-PV ML study. The excerpt also does not document any specific missing-data procedure for an original student-level re-analysis, so missing-data handling is treated as not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper does not report a single unified student-level analytic sample. Instead, it describes the availability of repeated cross-sectional observation points across IALS (1994/1996/1998), ALL (2003/2007), and planned/ongoing PIAAC waves for adults aged 16–65, and it provides country-specific trend analyses for Australia and the Netherlands (with additional countries referenced in an annex). For the purposes of the described trend approach, the relevant filtering is at the survey-wave level (selecting comparable literacy/numeracy/problem-solving measures across IALS/ALL/PIAAC and focusing on working-age adults 16–65), rather than a documented microdata inclusion/exclusion rule set.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper reviews and synthesizes evidence on how cognitive foundation skills relate to ageing, and it explains how repeated cross-sectional adult literacy measures from IALS (1994–1998) and ALL (2003–2007), together with future PIAAC observations, can be used to estimate skill gain and skill loss at the cohort level. It emphasizes that cross-sectional age differences are confounded by cohort and period effects, while longitudinal designs face retest and attrition biases; repeated cross-sections can help distinguish ageing effects (within-cohort change) from cohort effects (between-cohort change) when samples are representative. The paper reports that pooled IALS/ALL profiles show negative relationships between literacy proficiency and age across working-age adults (16–65), with education adjustment changing the pattern (differences become smaller from mid-20s to mid-50s). For Australia and the Netherlands, it describes statistically significant cohort and ageing effects at specific ages, but it does not provide ML model performance metrics or a documented PV/missing-data/weighting strategy for an original predictive analysis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is treated as a review/overview rather than an empirical ML study: the excerpt contains conceptual/theoretical discussion and descriptive trend evidence, but no student-level predictive modeling pipeline, no reported ML algorithms, and no PV-based outcome modeling with documented PV/missing-data procedures. Therefore, fields such as total_students, per-country analytic Ns, and ML technique performance metrics are not extractable from the provided text.
